takeaway: Giddens ties trust to accepting risk, while Luhmann ties it to ignoring complexity.
explain_script: Giddens and Luhmann both write about trust but mean different things by it. Giddens says trust is what lets you act despite risk you can't fully know. Luhmann says trust is what lets you ignore most possible futures so you can act at all.

nodes.label: Giddens
nodes.one_line: Says trust is confidence in reliability despite risk.

nodes.label: Luhmann
nodes.one_line: Says trust reduces complexity by ignoring most futures.

nodes.label: trust
nodes.one_line: The shared idea both theorists define in incompatible ways.

nodes.label: risk
nodes.one_line: The uncertainty Giddens says trust lets you act despite.

nodes.label: social complexity
nodes.one_line: The overwhelming number of outcomes Luhmann says trust filters down.

glossary.plain_definition: The recent historical period shaped by industrial, rational society.
glossary.in_this_passage: The era where both theorists say trust becomes especially important.

glossary.plain_definition: Ignoring most options so you can decide at all.
glossary.in_this_passage: How Luhmann says trust works: it filters out most possible futures.

simplifications: Flattens a longer disagreement about modernity into a single contrast over trust.
Treats risk and complexity as fully separate when the theorists' accounts overlap.
